articles.body: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after 26 years, with global health authorities confirming that the highly contagious disease has become endemic again in the country amid a surge in infections and declining vaccination rates.According to The Guardian, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional branch of the World Health Organization (WHO), announced the decision on Tuesday. The development comes as the US faces its worst measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 5,400 cases and eight deaths reported in 2026.PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa said measles transmission had been re-established in the US, Mexico and Bolivia, pointing to persistent gaps in vaccination coverage across the Americas.“Measles is resurging globally amid the persistent gaps in vaccination coverage, and this global trend is also affecting the Americas,” Barbosa said.The loss of the designation means the US is no longer considered to have interrupted the continuous spread of measles within its population.What led to the loss of measles-free status?The resurgence has been linked to declining vaccination rates and the spread of misinformation about vaccines. The development has also renewed scrutiny of President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who have faced criticism over their statements on vaccine safety.Trump recently called for the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) combination vaccine to be split into separate shots, claiming without evidence that administering them together could be dangerous.Kennedy, who was a prominent voice in the anti-vaccine movement before joining the administration, has also faced criticism over his approach to vaccination.However, experts have cautioned against attributing the outbreak solely to the Trump administration, noting that misinformation about the MMR vaccine has circulated for more than two decades.Noel Brewer, a behavioural scientist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who studies vaccination behaviour, said the problem extended across North America.“The US has had large outbreaks and exported those to Canada and Mexico, and those cases have come back again to the US,” he said.The US is not the only country to have lost its measles elimination status. The UK and several European countries have also recently lost the designation amid a resurgence in cases and declining vaccination coverage.David Margolius of the Big Cities Health Coalition said the situation reflected a broader international trend, with vaccination rates declining and infections increasing across countries.What does losing the status mean for Americans?The loss of measles elimination status is more than a symbolic setback. It means the virus is once again spreading continuously within the US population, increasing the risk of infection for people who are not vaccinated.Earlier, most measles cases in the country were linked to infections brought in by international travellers. With endemic transmission re-established, people can now face a greater risk of contracting the disease within their own communities.Health officials have also urged Americans to locate their old vaccination records, with some potentially facing quarantine requirements of up to 21 days.Public health leaders have described the development as a major setback, particularly because measles is preventable through vaccination.The Big Cities Health Coalition, which represents health departments serving 47 million Americans, said declining vaccination rates had opened the door to outbreaks, preventable illnesses, hospitalisations and deaths.Brewer said restoring the country's elimination status would require a national plan with clearly defined responsibilities. He also called for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the president to publicly support vaccination, alongside greater funding from Congress.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ex-hostage recounts captivity in Iran-backed militia stronghold now targeted by Iraqi prime minister
articles.summary: Israeli-Russian researcher Elizabeth Tsurkov describes where Iran-backed Iraqi terrorists held her captive for months as Iraq's Trump-backed prime minister orders a crackdown on the militia.
articles.body: An Israeli-Russian researcher held hostage for 903 days by an Iran-backed Iraqi terrorist group revealed to Fox News Digital that she spent the first four and a half months of her captivity inside the very militia stronghold Iraq's Trump-backed prime minister has now ordered the army to reclaim. Elizabeth Tsurkov, a senior nonresident fellow at the New Lines Institute for Strategy and Policy, said Kata’ib Hezbollah turned a private family's home in Jurf al-Sakhr, south of Baghdad, into a prison where she was held captive. "This is where I was held for 4.5 months," Tsurkov told Fox News Digital in an interview, referring to the early months of her captivity, which began with her abduction in Baghdad in March 2023. "I was held in a private home of a family that was taken over by Kata’ib Hezbollah and turned into a prison," she said. TRUMP ADMIN WARNS IRAQ OVER IRAN TERROR PROXIES AS US REPORTEDLY BLOCKS CASH PAYMENTS Tsurkov, who was freed in September 2025 following negotiations and sustained pressure from the Trump administration to secure her release, said that any effort to reclaim the territory must go far beyond dismantling alleged oil-smuggling operations. She called for Iraqi authorities to search the sprawling area, including surrounding towns and villages, for "secret prisons," "mass burial sites" and "storage facilities for weapons," and to return confiscated homes to their rightful owners. The revelations come as Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who has received strong public backing from President Donald Trump, ordered Iraqi armed forces into Jurf al-Sakhr, also known as Jurf al-Nasr, a stronghold of the U.S.-designated terrorist organization Kata’ib Hezbollah since 2014. According to AFP on November 16, Baghdad has given the militia a deadline to withdraw, with a security source identifying Friday. The order follows a Reuters investigation published Monday, citing Iraqi officials who accused Kata’ib Hezbollah of stealing hundreds of millions of dollars in state-owned oil since 2021. The government has dismissed nine security and administrative officials and referred suspects to the judiciary. The militia denies wrongdoing. IRAN’S PROXY WAR HAS CROSSED OCEANS AND IS NOW KNOCKING ON AMERICA’S DOOR A territory beyond government control For Tsurkov, the stakes go far beyond oil revenues. She described Jurf al-Sakhr as a territory effectively closed to the Iraqi government since 2014, when Iran-backed militias helped drive ISIS from the area but prevented its predominantly Sunni population from returning. Tsurkov estimated that between 120,000 and 180,000 people were displaced from the district and surrounding communities. "If Iraqis are allowed to return to their homes, this would signal ... restitution of state sovereignty," she said. She explained that the current operation is being presented as an anti-corruption campaign rather than an attempt to dismantle Kata’ib Hezbollah's military infrastructure. The organization retains bases elsewhere in Iraq and access to border crossings with Iran, she said, giving it opportunities to replenish its weapons even if it loses control of Jurf al-Sakhr. IRAN-BACKED TERROR SUSPECTS PLOTTED ATTACK ON US TROOPS USING VANS PACKED WITH FUEL, DOJ SAYS A crackdown or another political performance? Michael Knights, head of research at Horizon Engage, a New York-based strategic consultancy, and an adjunct fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, expressed skepticism that Baghdad would fundamentally challenge the militias. "It's going to be very difficult to tell the difference between a real crackdown on Iran-backed militias and a fake one," Knights told Fox News Digital. Previous Iraqi governments have announced crackdowns on militias, only for detainees to be released or armed groups to retain control through rebranded security arrangements. In June 2020, when then-Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi ordered the arrest of 14 Kata’ib Hezbollah members. Armed militia supporters subsequently descended on Baghdad's fortified International Zone demanding their release. Most were later released, according to a U.S. government inspector general report. In Nov. 2021, Kadhimi survived an explosive-drone attack targeting his residence. Reuters reported that security officials implicated Iran-backed militias, although no organization claimed responsibility. Knights said that the Iraqi counterterrorism forces are better trained and equipped than Kata’ib Hezbollah, but the greatest danger lies in the militias' ability to threaten officials and their families. "It's not about equipment or even training," he said, describing the danger of retaliation against commanders and their families who challenge the armed groups. In a Nov. 16 Middle East Forum analysis, researcher Ali Mahmoud detailed competing allegations of corruption between Kata’ib Hezbollah and Asa’ib Ahl al-Haq, including claims involving companies connected to militia leaders' families. Mahmoud reported that even the government's initial inspection of Jurf al-Sakhr required negotiations with senior militia commanders, illustrating the limits of Baghdad's authority. IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS What captivity revealed about the militia Tsurkov, who has researched Iraqi armed groups for years, said her captivity gave her unusual insight into the organization's internal culture. "I interacted with about 45 different individuals across basically three different prisons," she said, explaining that she later supplemented those observations with interviews involving former militia members and people familiar with their communities. Her conclusion was that the organization consists of both deeply committed Iranian loyalists and a much larger group of recruits primarily motivated by salaries, status and the ability to exercise power. "They enjoy having power over others," she said, describing what she observed among her captors. While some members embrace Iran's revolutionary ideology, Tsurkov said many joined after the major fighting against ISIS ended, attracted by government-funded salaries and relatively secure employment. "They're not interested in dying in the service of the Iranian regime," she said of many rank-and-file fighters. She distinguished those recruits from a smaller core of ideologically committed and better-trained operatives that Iran can mobilize for sophisticated military attacks. That distinction, she said, could offer Baghdad a path toward reducing militia power without a full-scale confrontation. She proposed allowing some fighters to join the regular Iraqi army under independent military commanders, providing alternative employment while dismantling their existing command structures. US FACES ANOTHER MAJOR MIDDLE EAST TROOP WITHDRAWAL, BUT THREAT REMAINS Iran's enduring influence According to Knights, the current crackdown primarily affects the more confrontational Abu Hussein wing of Kata’ib Hezbollah, while another faction associated with senior militia commander Abu Fadak remains largely untouched. He argued that both ultimately remain responsive to Tehran. Knights also questioned whether disrupting one oil-smuggling operation would substantially weaken the group's finances, citing its extensive investments in hotels, property and other commercial ventures. But perhaps the clearest illustration of the contradictions facing Iraq's government, Knights said, lies in recent senior political appointments and Iran's choice of its next diplomatic representative in Baghdad. On Oct. 15, Iraq's parliament approved Laith al-Khazali, a senior figure in the Iran-backed Asa’ib Ahl al-Haq militia, as one of three deputy prime ministers. The United States designated him and his brother Qais al-Khazali, the militia's leader, as specially designated global terrorists in 2020. Washington has accused the organization of carrying out attacks against American and coalition forces, according to al-Monitor. IRAN'S SHADOW OPERATIONS STRETCH ACROSS EUROPE AS CHILLING SPY CONVICTIONS EXPOSE TEHRAN'S REACH Another newly appointed deputy prime minister, Muhsin al-Mandalawi, is the brother of two Iraqi businessmen sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department on Sept. 10 for facilitating financial transactions benefiting Iran. Knights also pointed to Iran's reported selection of Abdolreza Meskarian, a senior commander in the Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force, as its next ambassador to Iraq. Alhurra reported on Nov. 9, citing an Iraqi Foreign Ministry source, that Tehran nominated Meskarian, who heads the Quds Force's Ramadan Headquarters, a unit involved in coordinating with Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq. Neither government had formally confirmed the nomination. For Knights, these developments raise fundamental questions about how far Baghdad is prepared to go in challenging Tehran's influence. "I think on balance, we're still in a pretty bad place in Iraq when it comes to militias," he said. IRAN’S PROXY MONEY MACHINE: HOW THE HOUTHIS BUILT A MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR NETWORK DESPITE US SANCTIONS The real test Tsurkov agreed that an operation intended merely to satisfy Washington could be exposed if displaced families remained unable to return. The broader disarmament deadline, already extended until June 2027, was "utterly unrealistic," she said, arguing that Iraqi security institutions would require years of reform before they could reliably confront the militias. "I tend to think it will not be real," she said of the current operation, while acknowledging that successful government control could represent a meaningful breakthrough. For the former hostage, the ultimate measure of success is straightforward: whether Iraq's military merely enters the area, or whether the territory truly returns to civilian control. "It's either the state is there, and people can return or not," she said. Still, he acknowledged the possibility that the confrontation could mark the beginning of a broader effort, even if he doubts this particular operation will prove decisive. "Every great journey starts with the first step," he said.

articles.title: Government backs welfare shake-up to prevent 'lost generation'
articles.summary: Ex-minister Alan Milburn has set out plans to divert spending from benefits towards job support.
articles.body:
The government has backed plans by former minister Alan Milburn for sweeping reforms to prevent "losing a generation" of young people to a life on benefits.

Milburn proposes spending billions on tailored support for under 25s not in employment, education or training (Neets), to be part-funded by cuts to some benefits.

He claims his plan, which also proposes tax breaks for firms and major education reforms, will get 440,000 young people into jobs by 2036.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he endorsed the "principles" of the Milburn review and was confident he could persuade Labour MPs to back legislation to implement its measures.

The PM told Sky News he would set out a full response to the review next month, after he had received a separate report into Personal Independence Payments (Pips) by Social Security Minister Sir Stephen Timms.

But he added: "I have never in my years in politics seen a wholesale, whole government approach to supporting the next generation.

"That is what this represents, and I am absolutely confident that I can take this vision and get people behind it, indeed get the country behind it, because we will not place Britain in the position I want it to be in if we have a generation of young people growing up without hope for the future."

The government has made Milburn the head of a new new youth opportunities unit to deliver on his recommendations.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said her party agreed with Milburn's "diagnosis" but claimed Labour had "made the problem much worse for young people" by increasing employers' National Insurance contributions and the youth minimum wage.

There are few signs so far that Burnham will face a backlash from his own MPs of the scale that blocked his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer's planned £5bn welfare cuts last year.

But some left-wing Labour MPs and the Unison trade union have warned proposals to cut health-related benefits will drive some young people into poverty.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told MPs that "in future" the welfare state should be judged "not just by a snapshot of people's monthly incomes" but "but by the story of people's lives, and by their ability to achieve their full potential".

McFadden, who was flanked by Burnham and Chancellor John Healey during his statement in the Commons, said the government rejected claims that young people were "snowflakes and shirkers".

The million who were not in work or training had been robbed of the "prospect of a good future" and that was something that demanded "much more" than a conventional government response, he told MPs.

He said the government would publish draft proposals on welfare reform early next year, with legislation to follow.

In his wide-ranging 250 page report , Milburn proposes:

An "entirely new benefits system" for under-25s, which would end the health-top up of Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payments (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales

Instead, a new "youth allowance" would be set at the basic rate of Universal Credit for under-25s, with a higher rate for those living independently

A reduction in employers' National Insurance costs for 21- to 24-year-olds, starting in the retail and hospitality sectors, meaning employing those young people would be cheaper

A huge expansion in post-18 college places and a legal right to work, education or training

A new, locally-led Youth Opportunity Service in England to give young people one named advisor and a personalised participation plan

Primary and secondary schools required to identify and support pupils at risk of becoming Neet, and schools obliged to offer work experience

The report calls for the government to spend around £5.8bn in total by 2036-37 on extra mental health and employment support.

And it urges ministers to "kickstart the reform programme" next year, with an initial £500m, from "repriotising" existing spending.

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report

Why Milburn's Neets reforms will only save £200m a year by 2036

Where are the most jobs for 18-24 year-olds?

Milburn has said his plans are not about saving money - and his report says the government will not see overall savings from reduced benefit bills and higher tax receipts until 2036/27, when it will claw back £200m.

But by then, it assumes the share of 16–24-year-olds that are Neet will have gone down from 13% - one of the highest in Europe - to 5%, the lowest in the UK since records began.

Launching his report earlier on Tuesday, Milburn said "half measures will not do" because "the scale of the problem is just too big for that".

He added: "Britain is at risk of losing a generation of young people, not because they lack talent, not because they lack ambition, not because they do not want to work.

"This is not a crisis of aspiration; it is a crisis of opportunity."

Milburn's report has no specific blueprint for Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, where education, skills, health and local government are devolved.

He said the UK and devolved governments "should agree common definitions, a shared set of headline outcomes and a regular joint review of progress".

Scotland's Education Secretary Màiri McAllan said: "Where there is opportunity to collaborate with the UK government and others for the benefit of young people in Scotland, we will take it."

But she argued many of the reforms recommended for England, such as stronger vocational training, were already in place in Scotland.

A spokesperson for the Welsh government said: "We stand ready to work with the UK government to ensure Wales benefits fully from any UK-wide measures that improve life chances through access to rewarding work."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said he agreed "with the general drift of the Milburn report, but it's too little and too slow".

"We have a fundamental problem in Britain," he added. "Too many people are being encouraged to go on benefits, and training and apprenticeship schemes that take far too long."

Lib Dem treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said if the government wanted to get people into work, it should back high street firms "that give many their first job", scrap the "unfair jobs tax" and negotiate a new growth and defence partnership with the EU.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski described Milburn's proposals as a "flimsy sticking plaster" that intend to "slash support for disabled young people while subsidising corporations to hire cheap labour".

articles.title: M8 westbound reopens after bus bursts into flames near Livingston
articles.summary: Footage shows large flames engulfing the vehicle and there were reports of long queues.
articles.body:
The M8 westbound has reopened after a bus burst into flames during rush hour.

The busy motorway was closed between junctions two and three after the fire was reported at about 16:55.

Traffic Scotland said the road had now reopened.

Footage showed large flames engulfing the vehicle and there were reports of long queues stretching back to Hermiston Gait in Edinburgh.

The Scottish Fire Service said two fire engines attended the scene.

Police Scotland said there were no reports of injuries.

articles.title: Illinois man charged in connection with bomb found at Peoria ethanol plant
articles.summary: An Illinois man who worked as a trainee at a Peoria ethanol plant was charged Tuesday by a federal grand jury with two felonies related to a bomb that was found at the facility, resulting in a mass evacuation.
articles.body: An Illinois man who worked as a trainee at a Peoria ethanol plant was charged Tuesday by a federal grand jury with two felonies related to a bomb that was found at the facility, resulting in a mass evacuation. Police said they found a bomb on Friday at the BioUrja facility and “rendered it safe” before allowing residents who had been evacuated to return on Saturday. Hundreds of people who live within a 1-mile radius of the industrial site were evacuated. Andrew Kozak, 41, of Chillicothe, Illinois, was charged by the grand jury in federal court with making threats involving explosives, a felony punishable by 10 to 25 years in prison. He was also charged with making that threat to BioUrja Renewables over email, a felony punishable by five to 10 years in prison. Kozak has been a trainee at the facility for 10 months, according to his LinkedIn page. “Learning how to operate an ethanol plant,” Kozak wrote under his job description. Police said the suspect was arrested at the BioUrja facility on Monday morning. They did not name Kozak at the time of his arrest. No attorney was listed for Kozak on the federal court website. He was scheduled to make his initial appearance in federal court in Peoria on Tuesday afternoon. The criminal complaint detailing the charges against Kozak was sealed. The U.S. attorney’s office in Peoria did not immediately return a message seeking comment. The BioUrja plant contains ethanol and “other highly combustible types of chemicals,” Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told WMBD-TV on Friday. It is not unusual for law enforcement to receive bomb threats and suspicious package calls, but they often don’t result in a credible threat even though such calls are taken seriously by officials who must assess and investigate the claims. Peoria, with a population of around 110,000, is located about 150 miles (about 240 kilometers) southwest of Chicago. Kozak lives about 15 miles north of Peoria.

articles.title: Remains of Danielle Lopez, woman who vanished 2 years ago, found in New Jersey Pine Barrens
articles.summary: The remains of a 37-year-old woman who vanished more than two years ago in the New Jersey Pine Barrens were found Saturday during a multiagency search, state police said.
articles.body: The remains of a 37-year-old woman who vanished more than two years ago in the New Jersey Pine Barrens were found Saturday during a multiagency search, state police said. A search operation was being conducted within the Brendan T. Byrne State Forest in Burlington County in connection with the April 2024 disappearance of Danielle Lopez. A forensic examination identified the remains as belonging to Lopez, New Jersey State Police said in a news release Monday. A cause and manner of death were not released, and police said the case remains active. Lopez was last seen on April 13, 2024, by witnesses who saw her walking on Lost Lane, a dirt road in a heavily wooded area in Woodland Township, authorities previously told NBC’s “Dateline.” A detective said her car was found on the road in a large puddle of water. Some of Lopez’s personal belongings were in the car, but police found no signs of suspicious activity. Authorities searched the area but did not find Lopez. About a year and a half ago, James Ramsey, a New Jersey private investigator, began looking into Lopez’s case, according to NBC Philadelphia. Ramsey told the news outlet that he received information last week about where Lopez’s remains were possibly located. Ramsey said police already had a large-scale search planned when he received that information. Her remains were found in a location that investigators had previously searched, Ramsey said. He told NBC Philadelphia that the area has rough terrain. “Anyone who knows what the Pine Barrens in Jersey, it’s a labyrinth,” he said. “It’s a needle in a haystack.” Ramsey did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday. State police said no additional information was currently available. Lopez’s mother, Sue Quackenbush, remembered her daughter as someone who “loved people and was always thinking of someone else first.” “If everyone would follow Danielle’s lead with a random act of kindness — allowing patience at a traffic light, or buying a stranger’s coffee — and do it thinking that is what Danielle would do, that would be appreciated,” she told NBC Philadelphia in a statement.

articles.title: American soldier arrested in UK taken into US military custody
articles.summary: The Metropolitan Police say he has been taken into custody by the US Military over suspected national security and espionage allegations.
articles.body:
A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.

The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.

Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.

Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".

British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

The day after Tyner's arrest, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to.

"We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress."

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.

FBI director Kash Patel said an army officer was in custody "as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation" between the bureau, US Army and various UK partners.

"Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action," he said.

"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk."

US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath" they all take.

"Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he added.

articles.title: NSA attributes US network outage to routine ‘maintenance’ activities
articles.summary: Recent outage at NSA follows a series of unexplained disruptions across US communication and transportation services.
articles.body:
The United States National Security Agency (NSA) has said an outage affecting its internal communications network was due to “routine maintenance”, following a report by CNN.

The report, published on Tuesday and citing six unnamed sources, said there was no evidence that the outage was the result of a cyberattack. The incident follows a series of outages that have gone without explanation in recent days.

The network, known as NSA Net, allows employees of the US surveillance agency to share highly classified information internally, CNN said.

A spokesperson for the NSA downplayed the outage in a statement to Al Jazeera.

“The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the statement said. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational, and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”

The reported network disruption at the NSA follows several other major outages that have affected communication and transportation services in the US.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) temporarily halted all takeoffs in the country on Friday, claiming that a system upgrade caused a flight communication overload. The ground stop, which lasted more than four hours, was called out of an “abundance of caution”, it explained.

The tech giant Microsoft also announced that services such as Outlook and Teams were down last week.

More recently, on Monday, outages hit major banks, and United Airlines briefly suffered a system disruption that delayed some departing flights.

US President Donald Trump has played down the seriousness of those outages.

“Things like that happen,” Trump told reporters on Tuesday. “It’s fine.”

articles.title: Burnham to set out options next month for long-term EU relationship
articles.summary: The prime minister says he will set out options for the future "alongside" his 10-year economic plan.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has said he plans to set out his proposed options to reshape the UK's future relationship with the EU next month.

Downing Street had been facing pressure to specify when the prime minister would take this step, after he previously said he would do so "around" a summit taking place in Brussels this week.

Burnham will travel to the meeting with the EU this Friday, where both sides hope to unveil new agreements on food, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.

However, it's understood he will not indicate any preference at this stage which of the long-term options he could back in future.

Speaking to Sky News, he said: "I'm in a negotiation about improving the Brexit deal - that's what I'm doing this week. We'll see how it goes.

"And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU."

He added this would be set out "alongside" the 10-year plan for the economy that he has promised to unveil before Parliament breaks for Christmas.

Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU single market, customs union, or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.

Negotiations for the deals to be unveiled on Friday began under Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, but Burnham has indicated he believes the UK's Brexit deal needs to be revised further.

Making his first major foreign policy speech on Monday night, Burnham told his audience: "After the summit, we will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship".

"This will take time, and we will present those options and our assessment of them to inform decisions in the next Parliament."

In September, Burnham told the Labour Party conference he would "take the opportunity around the summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain's long-term relationship with our European partners".

Asked on Tuesday whether Burnham was now "hitting the brakes" and pushing any announcement of options back further into the future, a No 10 spokesman said earlier: "I don't accept that characterisation."

And speaking to Sky News, Burnham rejected the idea he was stepping back, arguing he was "doing exactly what I said".

"I will set out next month what the next phase looks like, and that is exactly what I said at my conference speech."

He also dismissed a suggestion made by former prime minister Boris Johnson that he would be wasting his premiership by reopening arguments about Brexit.

Johnson told the Daily Telegraph: "It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority.

"He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won't win – because the reality is that people are not fools."

Responding to his comments, Burnham said: "I just don't think he's an authority on these matters.

"I'm afraid I'm not going to listen to Boris Johnson on this particular matter. He burned bridges and created a lot of bad feeling, and consequently, Britain suffered as a result of that."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage MP said Burnham was "turning his back" on his constituents in Makerfield, where two-thirds of residents voted for Brexit in the 2016 referendum.

"We haven't taken the full advantage of Brexit and the idea of tying us back to single market rules overseen by the [European Court of Justice] is nothing less than a democratic outrage," he added.

articles.title: Nepal PM Balendra Shah to cut short 1st India visit from 3 days to 25 hours
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Nepal PM Balendra Shah has cut his first bilateral visit to India from three days to 25 hours on Nov 22-23, with Kathmandu seeking $2 billion
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Nepal PM Balendra Shah has cut his first bilateral visit to India from three days to 25 hours on Nov 22-23, with Kathmandu seeking $2 billion (Rs 18,000 crore) in grants and concessional loans for flood reconstruction and infra projects, besides improved access through Indian airspace for its international airports.The visit, at PM Modi's invitation, will focus on economic cooperation, connectivity and pending bilateral projects, although differences over Pancheshwar hydro project and the recruitment of Nepalese Gorkhas into the Indian Army under the Agnipath scheme are unlikely to be resolved.Shah is expected to arrive in Delhi Sunday afternoon and return to Kathmandu Monday evening. He will hold a 30-minute one-on-one meeting with Modi on Nov 23, followed by delegation-level talks, and meet President Droupadi Murmu and EAM S Jaishankar. The former Kathmandu mayor, who became PM in March, has declined an offer to visit Bengaluru or Ahmedabad. A visit to Uttarakhand has also been dropped, restricting his trip only to New Delhi.Officials did not explain why Shah curtailed his visit. The shortened itinerary marks a departure from previous visits by Nepalese PMs, which typically lasted three to four days and included engagements outside the capital."The PM wants the visit to deliver tangible results, particularly on flood reconstruction, hydropower and projects that have remained stalled for years," a source in the Rastriya Swatantra Party told TOI.Nepal's proposed $2 billion package includes $1 billion in loans, $500 million in grants and $500 million for reconstruction following the Aug 26 floods.You use AI every day. articles.title: Sam Hartman's ex compares him to asparagus, Lane Kiffin plays dumb & thoughts on Kirk Herbstreit
articles.summary: Sam Hartman's ex-girlfriend Lauren Blake Boultier says the Commanders practice squad QB has the "personality of asparagus" as he lands a dating show.
articles.body: 'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com. We made it, guys. It's GTA 6 week! Just kidding. I've never played Grand Theft Auto in my life, and I don't plan to start on Thursday. But I know some of you are really pumped about this, and I love that for you. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE After all, where in real life can you steal a sports car, pick up a prostitute and go bird watching all in the same day? Meanwhile, I'm living over here in the dark ages with Mario Kart on N64. Still the best video game ever created, and I'll die on that hill. Although Duck Hunt on the original Nintendo was pretty rad, too. I remember thinking the zapper gun was the coolest thing in the world. My, how far technology has come. Speaking of technology, did y'all hear the power grid is going down today? Or tomorrow. Or sometime in the near future. Pretty unfortunate for those of you who don't have a closet full of stockpiled food and a husband who knows bushcraft. And thank goodness I learned how to churn butter and make candles on my trip to Conner Prairie back in sixth grade. And if you're wondering if Conner Prairie is like Pioneer Village in "South Park," yes. Spitting image. Although if we could figure out the FAA situation before my anniversary trip to Costa Rica in January, I'd really appreciate that. Anyway, better knock out these Nightcaps before everything goes dark. Sam Hartman gets not-so-glowing reviews from his ex-girlfriend I'm just kidding, I'm not subscribing to the doomsday fear mongering. Not yet, anyway. No time for cyber attacks when we have football and reality TV to watch. And speaking of both of those things, how about Sam Hartman's ex-girlfriend just casually launching the funniest insult I've ever heard? After news broke that Sam would be featured on a dating show, Lauren Blake Boultier took it upon herself to let everyone know the Washington Commanders' backup backup backup QB has the "personality of asparagus." She did elaborate on that statement, explaining, "He's good for you, but he's not exactly the most exciting thing on the menu." Which actually makes him sound a little better. Like he's not a mean, cheating jerk or anything. He's just a little boring. And, you know, there are worse things. This definitely just feels like an attention play from Lauren to insert herself into the news cycle after it was announced that Sam would be the new "Bachelor." And it worked! Because here I am writing about her and embedding her Instagram posts. Good job, Lauren. Oh, and to further prove that her complaints about Sam are actually very stupid, she went on to explain — according to TMZ — that "Sam's life revolves around football, fishing and family ... joking his idea of an adventurous weekend is trying out a different fishing spot." Wow, this guy loves his family? And fishing?! The HORROR! Anyway, Sam, can we book you for an interview with OutKick OutDoors? Lane Kiffin forgot he coached the Tennessee Vols As a Vols fan, I want them to win every game. But if there's absolutely one game we CANNOT lose, it's this Saturday against Lane Kiffin and the LSU Tigers. As someone who was actually a student during the (very brief) Lane Kiffin era at Tennessee, there's a special disdain in my heart for that jerkface. DAN DAKICH RIPS INTO LANE KIFFIN AFTER LSU'S LOSS TO TEXAS ELIMINATES TIGERS FROM CFP PLAYOFF PICTURE If Sam Hartman is dull, healthy asparagus, then Lane Kiffin is gas station sushi. Briefly exciting, until you immediately realize what a terrible idea that was. Flashback to January 2010 when Lane tried to disappear under the cover of night to abandon the Vols for greener pastures at USC. The students caught onto his play, though, as we all chased him off campus with "Swiperboy" Renaldo Woolridge (UT basketball player turned rapper) live tweeting the whole thing. A few days later, Swiperboy wrote a song that said, "Baby girl, I would never leave you like Kiffin." You know that I'm a youngin' / but I would never leave without telling you its comin' / No fakes, No fibs, No bluffin' / Stay wit ya for a year then leave like its nothin'? My God, what a time that was. Truly, you had to be there. Anyway, now that Lane's unsuccessful coaching career has followed him to a half dozen different schools since he left Knoxville, he barely remembers totally screwing over Tennessee. "It didn't even cross my mind that I used to be there." Brother, your son's name is literally KNOX. The good news is, LSU's loss to Texas last week ensured Lane won't be participating in this year's College Football Playoff. The bad news is he still has a chance to ruin the Vols' season. Don't you dare let it happen, Tennessee. Don't you dare. Let's open the mailbag. 📩 Email: amber.harding@outkick.com (Send your thoughts, stories, tips, rants and photos of your dog.) 🐦 Twitter/X: @TheAmberHarding 📸 Instagram: @amberharding No, Kirk Herbstreit's dog shouldn't be at a steakhouse Look, I know everybody and their brother-in-law's neighbor has already weighed in on Kirk Herbstreit letting his dog, Peter, gobble a filet off a plate at a fancy steakhouse. But since I got several emails asking for my two cents, here it is. I am not, personally, grossed out by dogs in restaurants. Maybe it's because I eat my meals in a house full of German Shepherd fur (though we do vacuum every single day and religiously change the air filters). So for me, the issue is not cleanliness — it's the sheer entitlement of Kirk Herbstreit. According to the NYC Department of Health, non-service dogs are prohibited from indoor restaurant dining areas. Period. We have the same law here in Tennessee. Yet apparently, Kirk thinks those rules shouldn't apply to him because his dog is somehow more special than everyone else's. Some people are allergic to dogs. Some people just don't like dogs. And some people want to enjoy their $100+ date night meal without someone's golden retriever slurping up a steak off a plate in the next booth. And y'all know I ADORE my dog — like an unreasonable amount. Sure, I take him on vacation and to open-air patios (where dogs are permitted), and I love a dog-friendly brewery. If I could take Rocky to work with me and fly him around in a private jet like Kirk does with Peter, I'd do it in a heartbeat. I mean, HELLO. Look at this guy. But treating your dogs well is not the same as imposing them on everyone around you. Or thinking you're above the law. For people who are like, "Chill, it's not that serious" ...it is, actually. The ego and entitlement are off the charts with that guy. And, someday, somebody needs to have the balls to tell Kirk NO. Nightcaps dogs of the week And now for your weekly dose of dogs that don't eat filets off plates at high-end steakhouses. Cindy F. writes: My dog Pepper did not like being told she could not go outside! JCP writes: Penny — survived parvo! One more thing: Is 'Peppa Pig' always this funny? I don't have kids, so my knowledge of children's TV programming ended somewhere with "Rugrats." But I've been seeing this "Peppa Pig" scene floating around X, so I watched it. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER And it did not disappoint. The execution. The attitude. 10/10, no notes.

articles.title: US Navy chief says Iran war has put ‘strain’ on maritime forces
articles.summary: Lawmakers hound Hung Cao over expanding war, opaque leadership shake-ups, and low crew morale at confirmation hearing.
articles.body:
United States Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has acknowledged that the Iran war is taxing the maritime service as bipartisan senators questioned him over extended ship deployments, dwindling weapons stockpiles, and resources being shifted away from the Asia-Pacific.

Testifying before the Senate Armed Services Committee on Tuesday at his confirmation hearing to lead the military branch, Cao faced sharp, bipartisan grilling over the mounting human and material costs of the US-Israel war on Iran, which is now deep into its ninth month.

“This war, again, I know it’s a strain on our navy,” Cao said, while insisting that joint military efforts have “really set China back on their heels”.

Cao, a retired US Navy captain and former Republican Party candidate for the Virginia Senate, has served as acting navy secretary since April 2026 after previously holding the under-secretary post.

The candidate, backed by US President Donald Trump, is now seeking US Senate confirmation for the permanent top civilian job.

The hearing comes amid burgeoning political fallout over the protracted quagmire with Iran , which recently saw a failed US House bid to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his stewardship of the war.

Voter frustration over the war — and its economic sting — proved decisive in the November midterm elections, which were widely seen as a repudiation of the war and ultimately cost the Republicans control of both the House and the Senate.

The Democratic-controlled 120th Congress is scheduled to be sworn in on January 3, 2027.

As the ranking Democrat on the committee, Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island questioned Cao during the nearly two-hour hearing, saying he was candidly troubled by his performance so far.

“I am concerned, frankly, about your leadership record as acting secretary,” said Reed, who called on the acting US Navy secretary to speak to Hegseth ‘s ongoing and planned dismissals of numerous naval officers over the past year, pressing Cao on whether he would “defend the military leaders in the future from partisan meddling in their careers”.

Democratic lawmakers went on to criticise the US Navy for bypassing standard congressional notification after quietly relieving the entire leadership team — the commander, executive officer and command master chief — of the nuclear-powered attack submarine USS South Dakota following an October underwater collision with the seabed.

“We relieve commanding officers for everything from negligence to even just fraternisation or, you know, harassment,” Cao said, making the case against the US Navy’s traditional policy of publicly announcing the removal of commanders. “I want to make sure that we’re protecting their livelihood afterwards as well.”

His stated intent to safeguard individuals’ careers was promptly rebuked by Reed, who maintained that privacy does not justify shielding information from congressional oversight.

“The squadron commodore [of the USS South Dakota] felt that they did not live up to their honour, courage, and commitment ethos, and therefore, he relieved the commanding officer, the executive officer, and the command master chief,” Cao countered.

Cao’s record on sailor mental health comes under fire

The US Navy chief-nominee also faced intense questioning from lawmakers about low crew morale, severe supply shortages, and mental health strains aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln following its record-breaking 265-day deployment in the Pacific Ocean, South China Sea, Indian Ocean, and North Arabian Sea.

The vessel returned to Naval Air Station North Island in San Diego, California, in early October after the USS George Washington arrived on station to relieve it. Together with the USS George HW Bush and the newly arrived USS Theodore Roosevelt, the US is temporarily massing three carrier strike groups to bolster regional maritime security and tighten the months-long naval blockade against Iran.

Last week, Trump stated that further military strikes against Iran are “quite unlikely” and said the military component of the war was “effectively over” following discussions with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani. He noted, however, that the US military remains “locked and loaded” if conditions change.

During Tuesday’s hearing, Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, argued that Cao was “failing these sailors and their families”, and noted that his “confrontation with them leaves me with the clear impression that you simply don’t care”.

Cao pushed back, declaring that he does not control the deployment lengths of US Navy ships that have crept steadily closer to a full year at sea — up from a standard of six to eight months during the US’s so-called “war on terror”.

“Sustained investment in our people will increase readiness, improve retention and recruitment, and enable our ability to support national objectives,” said Cao.

When asked about suicide attempts aboard the ships, Cao told Blumenthal that what he saw “as eight suicide attempts, I see as eight suicide mitigations”.

Cao faces a rare waiver hurdle for the top spot

In his opening statement, Republican Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker expressed support for Cao’s nomination to lead the US Navy, noting that while the service faces significant challenges during a particularly volatile time, it also has major opportunities.

Beyond fielding tough questions from lawmakers on Tuesday over the strain of the Iran war on fleet readiness, Cao still faces a complex confirmation path to become the permanent secretary of the navy, requiring a rare congressional waiver.

Because he left active-duty service in October 2021, he falls short of the seven-year separation period mandated by federal law to preserve civilian control of the military.

Securing that exemption poses a steep political climb for Cao, who must clear the hurdle by meeting a 60-vote threshold, which may prove tricky in a polarised Washington.

Cao will ultimately need cross-party support from Democrats or independents to avoid a filibuster, while winning over war-sceptical Republicans .

articles.title: Whistleblower: Deadly drone strike in Kuwait could’ve been avoided
articles.summary: Whistleblower accuses military of dismissing advanced security warnings of drone strike that killed six US soldiers.
articles.body:
Washington, DC – An American soldier wounded in a deadly Iranian drone attack in Kuwait is accusing senior military officials of ignoring warnings and being ill-equipped ahead of launching the US-Israel war on Iran, according to a whistleblower complaint.

The complaint, obtained by Al Jazeera English on Tuesday, is tied to an Iranian one-way attack drone that evaded air defences at the outpost within the first 48 hours of the war. Six service members were killed, and dozens were injured, including the whistleblower. It remains the deadliest assault on US forces since the war commenced.

The 14-page letter, submitted on Friday to the House and Senate Armed Services committees, alleges that the army repeatedly brushed aside warnings that the Port of Shuaiba in Kuwait was vulnerable to drone attacks. Though the site was fortified, there was no roof.

“The drone threat to the port was raised directly to the commanding general of the 1st Theater Sustainment Command at least three times in the week before hostilities,” the complaint states.

The soldier, who is not named, also alleges the installation had “no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance”, adding that at least one of those killed “could have survived” if there was adequate medical support on site.

The army says it has completed its investigation of the Port of Shuaiba attack but has not publicly released its findings.

In a news conference following the incident, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth described the drone as a “squirter” that “happened to hit a tactical operations centre that was fortified”.

But senior military leaders have acknowledged that Iran’s Shahed attack drones, known to fly low and slow, have inflicted more damage on the battlefield than anticipated.

Tehran has repeatedly targeted US and allied assets with attack drones and ballistic missiles. As a result, more than 23 American service members have been killed.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the allegations.

articles.title: Brother hopes to bring attention to disappearance of Missouri woman Megan Latham, last seen seven months ago
articles.summary: Megan Latham is believed to have last been seen on April 17 in Caledonia, Missouri. The 39-year-old was reported missing to the Washington County Sheriff’s Office, which is investigating her disappearance.
articles.body: Seven months ago today, 39-year-old Megan Latham was last believed to have been seen in Washington County, Missouri. Her family has been searching for her ever since. Jeremy Latham told Dateline his younger sister lived at home with him and their parents in Cadet, Missouri. “She’s a strong-willed individual,” he said. “Good at singing.” Megan was a registered nurse but was not working at the time of her disappearance. Jeremy last saw Megan on the evening of Thursday, April 16. “She was just sitting in her room,” he said. Authorities believe Megan was seen the following day in Caledonia, about a half-hour’s drive south of Cadet. “Whenever she didn’t come back after the weekend,” Jeremy explained, “my parents went to the police station.” According to Jeremy, his parents reported Megan missing to the Washington County Sheriff’s Office on Tuesday, April 21. A few weeks later, the Washington County Sheriff’s Office (WCSO) shared a press release on Facebook to provide an update in Megan’s case. According to the release, Megan was believed to have been seen at the intersection of State Highway 21 and State Highway 32 in Caledonia on April 17 between approximately 1:30 and 2:30 p.m. “Information gathered indicates she may have continued traveling south on State Highway 21 into Iron County,” the release states. The WCSO is working with the Iron County Sheriff’s Office to locate Megan. According to Jeremy, a detective interviewed people in the Caledonia area where Megan was believed to have last been seen, hoping to piece together her movements. One possible sighting placed Megan at a local restaurant. “I think she just stopped in to get a water,” Jeremy said. Another possible lead placed her at Elephant Rocks State Park in Iron County, about 10 miles from Caledonia. “Someone told my cousin that they seen her down by Elephant Rocks,” he said. Dateline spoke with Detective C.K. Wakefield of the Iron County Sheriff’s Office who says a deputy from Iron County went down to check out the scene at Elephant Rocks and Megan was nowhere to be found. He also noted that his department helped locate two persons of interest in Iron County who Washington County detectives then interviewed. Wakefield could not share any additional details about the investigation and deferred to Washington County for any other information. Dateline reached out to the Washington County Sheriff’s Office, but has not yet heard back. Jeremy told Dateline he, his parents, and one of his friends went driving and walking around looking for Megan. But they found no sign of her. “She left with just the clothes on her back,” he said. Jeremy says Megan’s phone was left at home, and the WCSO is now reviewing it for possible leads. Jeremy worries about what may have happened the day Megan vanished. “She could have maybe went to the woods somewhere and never came back out,” he said. “Or someone picked her up.” While he hopes his sister is just off with a friend somewhere, Jeremy has a sinking feeling based on how much time has passed. “Seems like something ain’t right,” he said. Jeremy wants to bring more attention to his sister’s case. “Hoping to get the word out and hoping that she’d see it and give us a call or something,” he said. If Megan is reading this, Jeremy wants her to know how her family feels. “We love her,” and “miss her right now.” Megan is around 5’5” and 175 lbs., with brown hair and blue eyes. She has a phoenix tattoo on her rib cage and several tattoos on her arm. She was last seen wearing a black long-sleeved shirt and gray sweatpants. If you have information about Megan’s disappearance, please contact the Washington County Sheriff’s Office at 573-438-5478. If you have a story to share with Dateline, please submit it here.

articles.title: Oldest known Pearl Harbor survivor dies at age 106 after lifetime of service to America
articles.summary: The oldest known Pearl Harbor survivor, Freeman Johnson, has died at 106 at his home in Massachusetts. The Navy machinist escaped the Japanese attack aboard the USS St. Louis.
articles.body: The oldest known survivor of the 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor has died at age 106. Freeman Johnson, who served aboard U.S. warships during some of the most pivotal moments of World War II, died Saturday at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts. His daughter, Diane Johnson, confirmed his death to The Associated Press (AP). Freeman Johnson was among an estimated 87,000 U.S. military personnel on Oahu when Japanese forces attacked Pearl Harbor on Dec. 7, 1941, according to the AP. HISTORIC US SHIP THAT ONCE RULED THE ATLANTIC FACES EXTRAORDINARY FATE NEAR FLORIDA He was 21 years old and serving as a Navy machinist aboard the USS St. Louis. Earlier that Sunday, Freeman Johnson had eaten breakfast and returned to his bunk to read while the ship awaited boiler repairs, The Boston Globe reported. When the attack began, Freeman Johnson initially mistook the sounds of gunfire for another Navy drill. He rushed below deck to his battle station, where he worked on one of the ship's boilers as the attack unfolded above him, according to the Globe. With the engines running, the St. Louis managed to escape the harbor and reach open water. By the time Johnson went above deck, Hawaii was no longer in sight, according to the Globe. Freeman Johnson continued serving throughout World War II, later joining the USS Iowa. The battleship transported President Franklin D. Roosevelt across the Atlantic in 1943 on his way to meet British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Josef Stalin, according to the AP. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER He was still aboard the USS Iowa when World War II ended. On Sept. 2, 1945, Johnson watched from about a mile away as Japan formally surrendered aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay, according to the AP. Despite his role in history, Freeman Johnson never viewed himself as a hero. He placed little importance on the medals he earned during his military service, he told the Globe in an interview earlier this year. "They're not for what you do, the way you think," Johnson said. "They're for where you've been." Life beyond Pearl Harbor After the war, Johnson returned to Massachusetts, where he married Ruth Hills and raised three daughters. The couple was married for 50 years before Ruth died in 2002, according to the Globe. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Now, as Thanksgiving approaches, Diane Johnson said she is thinking about her father being reunited with his wife and other loved ones. "It's going to be a hell of a Thanksgiving," she told the AP. "He's going to be up there with all of his friends and family and my mom." Diane Johnson, who lived with her father in Centerville, described him as "a good and humble man." Freeman Johnson remained active late in life, walking two miles a day until he was 102. When asked about the secret to his longevity, his answer was simple. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Just keep moving, that's all. Keep breathing," he told the Globe. articles.title: Apple outage: iCloud, Apple Pay and other services are being restored as the company works to get systems back online
articles.summary: If you're having trouble signing into iCloud or other Apple services today, you aren't alone.
articles.body:
Several Apple services suffered an outage today, preventing some users from signing into iCloud and using other Apple services. According to Downdetector , a site that tracks reports of online service outages, iCloud, Apple Support, Apple Pay, and the App Store all saw spikes in reports.

Apple's support page initially indicated issues with iCloud accounts and sign-ins, as well as other services. As of 3:52 p.m. ET, services appeared to be recovering, though the support page still showed some small issues.

According to Downdetector reports, these are the services that saw spikes in outage reports:

"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning," an Apple spokesperson told us in a statement. "We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible."

In addition to iCloud, Apple's support page also flags that AppleCare on Device, which lets you purchase AppleCare on your phone or tablet, is experiencing an outage. That's alongside Apple Business, Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps and Schoolwork

As of 1:10 p.m. ET, the page also listed the App Store and Apple Music as experiencing an outage. Around 1:41 p.m. ET, the affected services on Downdetector started showing a downward trend in reports, indicating they may be recovering.

Users online reported being signed out of services and unable to sign back in. Others reported being unable to activate new iPhones.

The issues follow a string of outages that have plagued online services over the past week. On Nov. 12, Microsoft Outlook and Teams were knocked out for more than 30 hours due to what Microsoft described as a technical issue. On Nov. 13, a technical issue caused all air traffic across the U.S. to be grounded , leading to thousands of canceled and delayed flights.

On Monday, online services at several major U.S. banks experienced problems for several hours after an issue with JPMorgan Chase's systems. Today, CNN reported that a highly classified communications network used by the National Security Agency (NSA) went down.

articles.title: Did Llwyneinion lagoon fire cause my husband's deadly cancer?
articles.summary: Steve Williams died of lung cancer 14 years after falling in to a lagoon at a toxic waste dump fire.
articles.body:
It was a sight which struck terror into the firefighters called to tackle it - a blazing chemical waste lagoon on fire, with barrels exploding into the air.

Steve Williams, then in his 20s, was one of 60 firefighters sent to tackle the burning Llwyneinion lagoon in August 1980, which was sending thick black smoke over a nearby village.

Steve slipped in and, although he was pulled out, his widow thinks what he swallowed may have cost him his life from a rare form of lung cancer aged 39. She said "someone should be held accountable".

Wrexham council, which owns the site, said while it did not meet the legal definition of "contaminated land", it regularly inspected and monitored the area.

A leading expert in fire chemistry and toxicity said it was difficult to establish a link between firefighters' exposure to chemicals and health issues later in life.

Steve's widow Jilska Williams believes the father-of-two's terminal cancer could have stemmed from the chemicals at the fire at the former toxic waste dump near Wrexham in north Wales.

"It's a definite probability," said the 71-year-old. "They're firemen and they're always running into fires, so you don't know what the long-term effects are going to be - but actually falling into the lake and drinking that fluid, which is full of chemicals. He had a double-whammy, didn't he?"

Steve's family are part of a group which came forward after the BBC documentary Buried with Michael Sheen highlighted Wales' toxic waste legacy.

They want surviving firefighters to be tested for deadly carcinogens they fear they were exposed to in the fire at the Llwyneinion lagoon.

Eleven firefighters or their families have told a BBC investigation about concerns the fire could have had an impact on their health.

They said there was an increased number of miscarriages suffered by partners of those who attended the fire in the year after - and also highlighted concerns about rates of cancers since.

Steve followed his dad into the fire service in 1978 and his first posting was in Wrexham, where he was among the first responders to the lagoon fire.

Jilska said he was checked at hospital after falling in, then given a tetanus injection before being sent home.

"What is a tetanus injection going to do for him?" said the retired nurse. "It was a disaster waiting to happen. A time bomb waiting to go off, as far as I'm concerned."

The couple moved to Melbourne in Australia, then in 1994 Steve was diagnosed with stage four cancer – small cell carcinoma - and given weeks to live.

He died three days after the couple's 17th wedding anniversary. Their children were aged six and 10.

The Llwyneinion site was a dumping ground for chemicals suspected to have included cancer-causing polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) from chemical giant Monsanto.

Sheen's Buried programme team found elevated levels of PCBs in soil samples taken in an area open to the public beyond the fenced-off lagoon, as well as at 13 other suspected dumpsites for the firm's toxic waste across the country.

PCBs were once widely used in things like lipsticks and white goods - and were liked for being non-flammable and hard to break down.

But today they are seen as the first "forever chemicals" which are building up in the environment, threatening wildlife and human health.

The Llwyneinion lagoon was purchased by the then Clwyd County Council for just £1 in May 1980.

Andy Moore spent the day bringing in foam to help firefighters smother the fire at the former dump - and saw Steve fall in.

Andy, who was also stationed at Wrexham, said firefighters were not equipped to face the chemicals in the lagoon.

"There was no request for chemical PPE, we were basically fighting that fire in our normal tunics, drips and helmets," said Andy, now 70.

"I was walking around that fire ground in a shirt and tie - I've always been concerned about what it could have done to me.

"I was diagnosed a year ago with skin cancer.

"Whether I can relate that back to this specific incident I don't know but there's too many coincidences - I talk to my colleagues and we've had a lot of our guys who have died young specifically of cancers."

Jim MacGrane was also a firefighter at Wrexham at that time and his wife suffered a miscarriage in the period after the fire.

"There were six wives that we can recall had miscarriages within 12 to 15 months of that incident," said Jim, now 71.

"It was highlighted by one of the guys on the station who said, 'that's not coincidence. There's something not right there'."

Mark Jones and his father Ken both attended the fire and Ken later died of lymph and brain cancer in 2011.

"Out of the 60 people that attended that fire a significant number had cancers or passed away with cancer," said Mark, now 68.

"I'd be keen to participate in some blood testing to see if there was any link because it's only recently we found out about the PCBs in the vicinity.

"We were fairly well looked after health-wise when we were in the service, we used to have an annual health check. Unfortunately once you've finished the service that doesn't continue."

Professor Anna Stec, one of the UK's leading experts on fire chemistry and toxicity, warned it would be challenging to prove a firefighter's exposure to particular chemicals during their career had led to health issues later in life.

"It's very difficult to link specific chemicals to health disorders and it requires a multi-disciplinary approach where we're looking at residents' exposure, their lifestyle, and so on," said the University of Leicester professor.

"With firefighters it's even harder," she added, as they can be exposed to "a cocktail of toxic substances" throughout their careers.

But Stec said there should be more research into what happened at Llwyneinion.

"What we're learning from our Firefighters' Cancer and Disease Registry is that we see a pattern where there is a major fire incident - and a group of firefighters developing similar cancers. So it's definitely worth looking at."

The Llwyneinion lagoon is still there, but fenced off, which has worried some of the firefighters.

"The actual lagoon is still there from what I can make out in the same state it was 46 years ago," said Stuart Jones. "The potential of that happening again is very clear."

The BBC has been told the group of Llwyneinion firefighters are set to meet with representatives from the Fire Brigades' Union (FBU) later this week.

"We're taking this really seriously," said Gareth Tovey of the FBU.

He said the union was consulting with scientists to "discuss what options we may have available to support" the retired firefighters in their search for answers.

Tovey said he would write to Wales' fire and rescue services to ask about protections in place today for those called to attend an incident at sites linked to historical dumping of toxic waste.

Eastman Chemical Company, which is responsible for Monsanto's legacy production in the UK, did not respond when asked to comment.

Wrexham Council said while the site did not meet the legal definition of "contaminated land" under current legislation, there were regular inspections of the surrounding area and ongoing monitoring of streams and groundwater.

"The council is sorry to hear of the illnesses experienced by members of the fire service and their families," said a council spokesperson.

The council said it took "its responsibilities for protecting public health and the environment extremely seriously" and had carried out "extensive investigations over many years" into the Llwyneinion lagoon.

Wrexham council added that concerns about the health of firefighters who attended the fire were raised with their contaminated land officer twice.

The first was in February 2004 by the fire officer in charge at Wrexham fire station and on another occasion by a fire officer, who was told to speak to the health authority.

On the risk of another fire on the site, Wrexham council said that in 2006 advice was sought from the fire service about this, but they were told a number of "specific circumstances" would need to occur for this to happen.

An emergency response plan has been drawn up, and it was revisited in 2017.

North Wales Fire and Rescue Service said it was not in a position to comment on the fire in 1980.

It added: "We recognise the importance of understanding the potential long-term health impacts associated with firefighting. Approaches to occupational health, wellbeing and health monitoring continue to be developed nationally as evidence, research and understanding across the sector evolve."

The Welsh government announced in its draft budget on Tuesday that it would commit £2m to "kick-start a new approach to managing contaminated land".

"We are developing a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land," the government said in a statement.

"We also continue to press the UK government for funding to address the legacy of Wales's industrial past, including the remediation of contaminated land."
